rows.claim: Synthetic-source domain adaptation is reported on three human pain-assessment benchmarks without using their pain labels for model training.
rows.target_variable: Dataset-specific UNBC PSPI facial-action score regression, BioVid four-class heat-stimulus recognition, and neonatal observer-rated binary pain/no-pain classification (N-PASS subset regression); no common endpoint
rows.population_or_data: UNBC-McMaster, BioVid, neonatal cohort
rows.verified_evidence: Publisher full text reports UNBC PSPI-score MAE 0.89 ± 0.09, BioVid four-class accuracy 78.3 ± 2.2%, and preliminary neonatal accuracy 81.5 ± 3.7%; Table 11 specifies N=120 video segments from 15 neonates and ~72% power.
rows.limitations: The paper describes 5-fold evaluation with no test-fold pain labels used for training, but §4.7 says Stage 2/3 used the full unlabeled real pool for all folds without excluding unlabeled frames from test subjects; authors call this an unquantified mild optimistic bias. Hyperparameters were tuned using a 5-subject UNBC subset. Each benchmark was used as unlabeled adaptation data in at least one condition, and the authors state none was a held-out external validation cohort. §4.3.4.3 calls neonatal data validation-only/not training, conflicting with §6.8.1.4 saying every benchmark was used for unlabeled alignment in at least one condition. Table 11 gives neonatal N=120 segments/15 neonates, while later figure captions report N=300 without reconciliation. UNBC PSPI is a facial-action score, BioVid is controlled heat-intensity classification, and neonatal labels are observer-rated procedure-associated pain assessments; these constructs are not interchangeable or direct measures of subjective pain.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Published synthetic-source unsupervised domain-adaptation feasibility on the reported benchmarks and protocols only. Do not call this independent external validation, clinical deployment validation, zero-shot learning without qualification, or evidence for Drosophila-to-human transfer.

rows.population_or_data: Adult Drosophila melanogaster, 2-5 days old, with freely walking behavioral groups tested separately by sex; calcium imaging uses an assay-specific n=5, while FANC/MANC connectome reconstructions are separate anatomical sources.
rows.verified_evidence: The 2025 bioRxiv v1 preprint reports an adult-fly optogenetic screen (Fig. 1), optogenetically evoked escape assays (Fig. 2), md-axon calcium imaging to a 40 C heat probe (Fig. 3), connectome analyses (Fig. 5), and optogenetic tests of candidate ascending pathways (Fig. 6). Different optogenetically activated pathways support rapid escape versus sustained place avoidance.
rows.limitations: This is a 2025 bioRxiv version 1 preprint, not peer reviewed. Heat sensitivity (Fig. 3) and escape/avoidance behavior (Figs. 1-2, 6) were tested separately; natural noxious heat was not shown to cause those behaviors. Candidate ascending pathways were tested by optogenetic activation only; necessity under natural stimulation was not tested, and no ascending-neuron recordings during natural stimulation were reported. Place avoidance/escape are behavioral readouts, not proof of subjective pain; no human/ECAP/SCS evidence.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Supports reported adult Drosophila nociceptive sensorimotor pathways and escape/avoidance behavior as preprint findings only. Do not interpret criteria-based pain framing as demonstration of subjective experience or human transfer.

rows.claim: Dynamic VNC connectome simulations nominate a compact walking-rhythm circuit; DNb08 activation evokes rhythmic, searching-like leg movements in decapitated flies.
rows.target_variable: rhythmic leg motor activity
rows.population_or_data: adult Drosophila VNC connectomes
rows.verified_evidence: The bioRxiv v2 preprint compares DNg100-driven front-leg motor activity across MANC, FANC, mCNS and BANC. Pruning finds a shared E1/E2-plus-inhibitory motif, but the minimal circuit varies by dataset (three interneurons in MANC; the common FANC circuit has four). The six-leg bilateral output and phase analysis are shown for full MANC; Extended Data Fig. 8 depicts all six MANC leg neuropils and only FANC front-left. DNb08 simulations produce rhythms in MANC, FANC and mCNS but not BANC; optogenetic activation in decapitated flies evokes searching-like rhythmic leg movements, not coordinated walking.
rows.limitations: Preprint (bioRxiv v2, 30 April 2026; PMC13142387.2), not peer reviewed. The exact minimal E-E-I circuit was obtained in MANC; other datasets yielded related but different circuits. The model's rhythms emerge from network connectivity without intrinsic bursting or pacemaker properties. DNb08 simulations produced rhythms in three of four datasets (not BANC). The optogenetic assay tests a fly motor pathway, not the exact four upstream matrix releases, nociception, subjective pain, human ECAP or SCS. The Abstract/Results generalize motif conservation across six legs and four connectomes, but the figure captions scope functional six-leg output to full MANC; four-dataset comparisons are front-leg subnetworks. Do not infer six-leg rhythmic output in each connectome.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Use as a connectome-simulation and fly motor-perturbation precedent; the biological comparison is limited to DNb08-evoked rhythmic leg movement.

rows.claim: Acute swine experiments show that epidural ECAP morphology depends on referencing and lead position and can mix with muscle EMG and stimulation artifact.
rows.target_variable: Epidural spinal recording ECAP morphology, amplitude/latency, stimulation artifact and concurrent EMG by reference and lead position
rows.population_or_data: Ten acute domestic swine (six male, four female); analysis-specific denominators include n=5 for reference comparisons and n=4 for lead-migration analyses.
rows.verified_evidence: Publisher full text reports ten acute domestic swine (six male, four female), two epidural Octrode leads, comparison of local-tissue/differential/contact referencing, and concurrent spinal and intramuscular EMG. Referencing changed artifact and ECAP magnitude; rostrocaudal lead shifts changed ECAP latency and strength in a four-animal analysis, whereas lateral shifts showed variable magnitude changes without a significant latency difference. Local muscle EMG could appear in epidural recordings. Recordings after euthanasia served as a control for separating neural ECAP from artifact or filter ringing. No predictive model or clinical analgesia endpoint.
rows.limitations: Acute animal electrophysiology only, with proprietary source data; referencing statistics use n=5 of the ten animals and lead-migration analysis n=4. The authors state the study was not preregistered and its findings are exploratory rather than confirmatory. No held-out-animal prediction validation, human pain outcome, clinical response or physical ECAP forward operator. Same consortium with substantial author overlap as S798, so related technical evidence rather than independent external validation.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Supports reference-, lead-position- and EMG/artifact-dependent epidural recording behavior in this acute swine setup only; does not establish human pain measurement or clinical SCS response.

rows.claim: In Drosophila larvae, low-threshold mechanosensory Cho input gates weak C4da nociceptor input at the C4da-to-A08n synapse, with A08n as the measured postsynaptic readout and modulates protective escape behavior in separate assays.
rows.target_variable: Separate readouts: heat- or C4da-evoked rolling; A08n electrophysiological depolarization/spikelets; Cho-terminal calcium activity; nociceptor-elicited crawling speed
rows.population_or_data: Drosophila melanogaster larval cohorts. Intact-larva behavior, opened/pinned whole-cell recording preparations and Cho calcium-imaging preparations are separate assays; no pooled study-wide sample size or animal-level cross-assay linkage is reported.
rows.verified_evidence: The primary article reports Cho inhibition increasing heat-evoked rolling at 27.5 C but not 39 C (Fig. 1A) and increasing C4da-evoked rolling (Fig. 1B-C). In separate whole-cell recordings, gentle touch suppresses A08n spikelets during weak C4da activation (Fig. 1E and Fig. 2A); Figs. 2B and 2D test complementary Cho manipulations; Fig. 2C is a C3da P2X2 negative control. The authors call these spikelets because some may not be action potentials. Cho-terminal calcium imaging confirms touch activates Cho (Fig. S1A-B). A separate dry-hard-agar assay reports increased nociceptor-elicited crawling speed in the early light-on period using a 0.5-second speed window (Fig. 4C-D). Fig. 1C groups contain 56-116 larvae per stimulus-intensity point; sample sizes otherwise are panel-specific.
rows.limitations: These results separate stimulus, neural-response and behavior assays: optogenetic C4da activation is not mechanical touch; A08n electrophysiology measures spike-like depolarizations, while calcium imaging measures Cho mechanosensory terminals, not C4da nociceptors; rolling and crawling are distinct behavioral outcomes. Preparations and cohorts are not linked at the animal level, and no pooled study N is reported. The study measures larval nociceptive processing and protective behavior, not subjective pain, human ECAP/SCS, clinical response or cross-species transfer. The proposed GABA-B R1 effect is at C4da presynaptic terminals through an unidentified GABAergic intermediary; A08n is the postsynaptic readout, not the demonstrated inhibitory locus. The ATR-free control uses C4da>ChR2-T195C at 300 µW/mm² (n=119), distinct from Fig. 1B-C's T159C; the variant/intensity difference is not reconciled.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Use as primary prior art for stimulus-dependent Cho-associated modulation of the C4da-to-A08n synapse of weak C4da input and associated larval protective behavior under the reported assays only. Do not infer subjective pain or human spinal/ECAP/SCS validity.

rows.claim: An author poster describes exploratory modeling of six-month SCS pain response from baseline variables in a prospective device registry.
rows.target_variable: Patient-reported reduction of at least two points on the 0-10 pain scale at six months after SCS implantation
rows.population_or_data: Product Surveillance Registry analysis of 721 back- and/or leg-pain patients enrolled in 2012-2023; conference abstract and one-page poster, with no accessible patient-level dataset.
rows.verified_evidence: The accessible one-page author poster defines response as at least a two-point pain reduction at six months, reports 721 registry patients enrolled from August 2012 through October 2023, an 80/20 training/test allocation, and five repeated five-fold cross-validation runs on the training set. It compares Elastic Net, random forest and XGBoost. Table 2 reports accuracy 0.680/0.691/0.685, sensitivity 0.862/0.940/0.819, specificity 0.354/0.246/0.446 and F1 0.775/0.796/0.769, respectively. The poster prose reports 274/363 responders in the combined back-and-leg-pain subgroup, while Table 1 reports 267 responders and 96 non-responders for that subgroup; both sum to 363.
rows.limitations: The direct ScienceDirect abstract route returned HTTP 403, but its publisher text was checked through a proxy. The abstract corroborates the 721-person cohort and 267/363 Table 1 value, while its snippet truncates before final model ranking and labels its Table 2 as optimal hyperparameters, unlike the poster's Table 2 of metrics. The poster itself contains an unresolved combined back-and-leg-pain subgroup discrepancy: prose 274/363 versus Table 1 267/363; neither is selected as a corrected figure. The poster does not permit verification of participant-disjoint split implementation, predictor-to-outcome linkage, calibration, or independent external validation; no patient-level dataset access is established. Random-forest specificity is only 0.246 despite sensitivity 0.940. No ECAP predictor or neural-recruitment measurement is stated. This is not evidence of a validated decision tool or an ECAP-to-pain mechanism.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Use only as poster-level prior art for exploratory registry-based responder modeling with the reported split and metrics. Do not cite a resolved subgroup count, ECAP-based prediction, external validation, or deployed clinical utility.

rows.claim: A small author preprint reports an association between baseline subcallosal cingulate structural connectivity and short-term SCS trial pain response.
rows.target_variable: More than 50% reduction in patient-reported VAS from before percutaneous SCS trial to 15 days after trial
rows.population_or_data: Eight patients with chronic low back pain recruited before an SCS trial (six UCLA, two UTSW); preprint version 1, data available only on reasonable request.
rows.verified_evidence: Methods Section 2.1 defines the eight-person cohort, 15-day VAS assessment and >50% response threshold. Methods Section 2.4 compares baseline SCC connectivity with binary trial response using a general linear model and continuous VAS change using Pearson correlation, with a separate regression including baseline HAMD. Results Section 3.1 reports the responder/non-responder VAS-change comparison as Z=-2.337, p=0.29 while describing it as significantly higher; this internal significance/p-value conflict is unresolved and is not treated as a supported group-comparison result. Section 3.2 reports connectivity associations in the same eight-person cohort, without a held-out predictive test. The primary Results §3.1 prints 81.25%±21.65 versus 14.44%±11.79, Mann–Whitney Z=-2.337 and p=0.29; the statistic and printed p disagree, and no correction is inferred. Results §3.3 prints SCC-VS b=-42.71, t(5)=-25.46, p=0.025, while the Abstract gives p=0.02 for this predictor; the t magnitude is inconsistent with the Results p.
rows.limitations: Non-peer-reviewed version-1 preprint; publisher landing page returned HTTP 403 on 2026-09-28, but the canonical publisher JATS XML was accessible and checked that day. Eight participants, only 15-day trial response. No independent validation, long-term post-implant outcome, public patient-level MRI/VAS dataset or ECAP measurement. Do not interpret association statistics as validated predictive accuracy or merge this cohort with other imaging studies without an identity bridge. Primary source discrepancies remain unresolved: the Abstract gives 6F/2M and age 70±10 for n=8, whereas the two Results §3.1 groups of four sum to 5F/3M with different age summaries. Printed significance values and cohort summaries cannot be silently reconciled.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Use as bounded prior art for baseline MRI connectivity associated with short-term SCS-trial VAS response; no claim of clinically validated prediction, ECAP-to-pain mechanism or durable treatment effect.

rows.claim: Poe et al. measured heat-probe-evoked rolling in larvae raised under different nutrient conditions, separately from C4da dendrite morphology.
rows.target_variable: Whole-larva 360-degree rolling responder fraction and latency after lateral A4 heat-probe contact; dendrite morphology is a separate endpoint.
rows.population_or_data: Wandering third-instar Drosophila larvae; Figure 6A-C reports 90 animals per high-/low-yeast group at each indicated temperature; Figure 6D-E reports 120 per group, with three repeats.
rows.verified_evidence: The eLife primary Methods specify a temperature-controlled probe on segment A4 and one test per larva. Figure 6A-E reports responder/fast-responder percentages and latency; C4da dendrite morphology is quantified in separate assays.
rows.limitations: The paper does not record stimulus-evoked neuronal firing or calcium during the behavioral probe assay; morphology cannot substitute for neural-response measurement. The larvae are not linked to human ECAP or SCS outcomes, and rolling is not a subjective-pain measure. Figure 6 legend says FoxO OE but the source-data workbook headers say foxo RNAi; the legend's n=120/group and three repeats also conflict with 120 versus 90 workbook rows. Genotype and denominator are unresolved, so no inference is drawn from the discrepancy.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Use as primary larval nocifensive-behavior and morphology comparator under the stated nutrient/genotype conditions only.

rows.claim: In a specified larval hot-probe assay, dTrpA1 RNAi did not alter the high-temperature withdrawal response relative to wild type, whereas thermotaxis was separately impaired.
rows.target_variable: Probe-evoked curling/withdrawal at approximately 55 C, distinct from thermal-gradient thermotaxis.
rows.population_or_data: Crawling third-instar Drosophila larvae in the hot-probe assay; Figure 3C group counts: uninjected n=41, dTrpA1 RNAi n=24, md-Gal4 n=23, UAS-TeTxLC n=30, md-Gal4:UAS-TeTxLC n=23. Figure 4H reports n=19 and n=20 for separate dTrpA1-Gal4 manipulations. No pooled study N.
rows.verified_evidence: The primary Results and Figure 3B-C state that larvae curled to a ~55 C probe, not to 25 C or 36 C probes, and that dTrpA1 RNAi larvae responded indistinguishably from wild type in this test. Figure 4H gives another assay-specific normal-withdrawal comparator.
rows.limitations: The negative result applies to the reported manipulation, genotype and probe assay; it does not show that dTRPA1 is irrelevant to all nociception. No stimulus-evoked neural activity recording, subjective pain, ECAP or clinical outcome is reported. S282 cites this work for dTrpA1 reagent provenance, not for this negative result.
rows.permitted_conclusion: Use as a bounded behavioral comparator separating thermotaxis from one high-temperature withdrawal assay.
